correctness.rationale: A full proof derives parity recognition for all factors of length >=3, then proves the suffix of length a quarter of the word occurs exactly three times using repeated aligned desubstitution to D_1 in D_3. Factor-type bijections for even/odd starts preserve multiplicities except omission of the terminal suffix occurrence. The threefold suffix protects all shorter factors from becoming unique. At odd length 2K+1 the four unique factors of preceding length K+1 lift bijectively to four at positions 2p+1. Base n=3 checked directly. Exhaustive independent factor-frequency computations for n=3..13 corroborate both main and suffix claims.

evidence: Banbara et al. Theorem 30: exactly two minimum size-two attractors of complete period-doubling words; Corollary 32: all occurrences of each factor of length at least three have fixed parity.
Charalampopoulos et al. Theorem 1.1: a general sublinear-time packed-string SUS algorithm.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A formula for optimum attractor sets does not determine occurrence multiplicities of individual factors; a generic algorithm for finding one SUS does not provide a closed form on a named family. Parity is a shared lemma and independently re-proved, not novelty claimed. The new exact three-copy suffix lemma and occurrence-preserving factor correspondence give the claimed count and starts.

value.rationale: For an established and algorithmically important morphic text family, the proof classifies every globally shortest unique substring across infinitely many text lengths, with exact length, count and positions. The sharp quarter-length-plus-one threshold and four-witness phenomenon provide explicit structural benchmarks for global SUS algorithms. This is a complete natural invariant, not a one-off small-instance check. No downstream implication beyond the stated classification is asserted.
